prompt: You stop at a four-way stop. A moment later a bakkie coming from your right also comes to a complete stop. Who may move off first?
options: The bakkie, because a vehicle on your right always has right of way
You, because you stopped first
Whoever is going straight rather than turning
explanation: At a four-way stop the order is decided by who stopped first, so you go before the bakkie. Yield-to-the-right only settles a tie when two vehicles stop at exactly the same moment, and going straight versus turning has nothing to do with the order.
note: Verified: duty to stop from NRTR 2000 reg 307(a). Arrival order is the K53 examiner standard, not a numbered regulation. Reg 301 yield-to-the-right applies to traffic circles, NOT four-way stops — that distinction is what this tests.

prompt: You are following a car on a dry, clear road. It passes a lamp post, you start counting, and you reach the same lamp post after about one second. What should you do?
options: Nothing — one second is enough on a dry road
Speed up and overtake so you are not stuck behind it
Ease off until the gap is at least two seconds
explanation: Two seconds is the minimum gap in good conditions, so a one-second gap is too close and you must drop back. One second is not enough on any road surface, and overtaking to escape a gap you created yourself just moves the problem instead of fixing it.
note: Checked NRTR 2000 for a numeric following-distance figure and found none — reg 298 covers passing only. The two-second gap is the K53 driving standard, not a statutory number.

prompt: The car ahead of you has stopped at a pedestrian crossing to let people walk across. The lane next to you looks clear. What may you do?
options: Stay behind it — you may not pass a vehicle that has stopped at a pedestrian crossing
Pass it on the right, as long as you can see your side of the crossing is clear
Hoot to warn the pedestrians, then pass slowly
explanation: A vehicle stopped at a crossing hides pedestrians from you, so the law simply does not allow you to pass it. Checking 'your side' is worthless when the stopped car is blocking your view of someone still walking, and hooting pressures pedestrians instead of protecting them.
note: Verified NRTR 2000 reg 315(4); yield duty is reg 315(2).

prompt: What is the correct order of checks before you change lanes?
options: Signal, then check your mirrors, then move
Check your mirrors, signal, check your blind spot, then move
Check your blind spot, move, then signal
explanation: Mirror, signal, blind spot, move — you gather information first, then tell others, then take one last look for what the mirrors missed. Signalling before you have looked commits you before you know it is safe, and signalling after you have already moved warns nobody.

prompt: You check your mirrors before changing lanes and they are clear. Why must you still look over your shoulder?
options: To show the examiner that you are alert
To check that your indicator is actually flashing
Because a vehicle can sit in the blind spot your mirrors do not cover
explanation: Mirrors leave a blind spot alongside and slightly behind you that is big enough to hide a motorcycle or a whole car, which is exactly what the over-the-shoulder look catches. It is a real safety check, not a performance for the examiner, and your indicator is confirmed on the dashboard, not over your shoulder.

prompt: You have finished changing lanes and your indicator is still flashing. What should you do?
options: Cancel it as soon as the lane change is done
Leave it on until you next turn
Leave it on — it warns drivers behind that you have just moved
explanation: An indicator left running tells other drivers you are about to move again, so cancel it the moment the manoeuvre is complete. Leaving it on until your next turn, or as a 'warning', feeds everyone around you false information about what you plan to do.

prompt: You signal in good time to pull out into the next lane. Does the signal give you the right to move across?
options: Yes — once you have signalled, other drivers must let you in
No — a signal only announces your intention, so you still have to make sure the lane is clear
Yes, provided you have signalled for at least three seconds
explanation: A signal warns others what you plan to do; it never creates right of way, so the mirror and blind-spot checks still decide whether you may move. There is also no magic number of seconds that turns a signal into permission — the law asks only that it is clear and early enough to warn.
note: Verified NRTR 2000 reg 300: signal must be 'of a duration sufficient to warn'; no fixed seconds, confers no right of way.

prompt: You are approaching a mini-circle and a car is already travelling around it. What must you do?
options: Enter the circle first if you get there before it finishes its turn
Stop completely and wait for every vehicle at the circle to leave
Give way to it and enter only once it is safe
explanation: Traffic already in the circle keeps moving and has right of way, so you give way and enter when there is a safe gap. Pushing in ahead of it cuts off a vehicle that is entitled to be there, and waiting for the circle to empty completely is not required and simply blocks everyone behind you.

prompt: You and another car reach an empty mini-circle at exactly the same moment. The other car is on your right. Who goes first?
options: The car on your right
You, because the car on your right must yield to you
Whoever is going straight through the circle
explanation: When vehicles arrive together at a circle, right of way goes to the vehicle approaching from your right, so you wait and let it through. The rule never runs the other way round, and what each driver intends to do after the circle makes no difference to who goes first.
note: Verified NRTR 2000 reg 301 (right of way at junctions where traffic moves around a traffic island).

prompt: You reach a mini-circle in a quiet suburb and there is no other traffic anywhere near it. What must you do?
options: Come to a complete stop, the same as you would at a four-way stop
Slow down enough to give way if needed, then drive through smoothly
Drive through at your normal speed, since a circle has no stop line
explanation: A circle asks you to yield, not to stop, so with nothing to give way to you slow down, check, and keep moving. A full stop is what a stop sign demands, and holding your normal speed leaves you unable to yield if a car does suddenly appear from your right.
note: Reg 301 imposes a duty to yield, not stop; reg 307(a) makes stopping compulsory only where a sign directs.

prompt: You are driving around a mini-circle and the next exit is the one you want to take. What should you do?
options: Nothing — indicators are not used inside a circle
Signal only once you have left the circle
Signal before the exit so other drivers know you are leaving
explanation: Drivers waiting to enter need to know you are coming out, so you signal before the exit while the message can still change what they do. Not signalling at all leaves them guessing, and signalling once you are already out is too late to be any use to anyone.
